newsitem.title: UK: Copper prices seen lower, stocks up in 97-98--EIU.
newsitem.headline: Copper prices seen lower, stocks up in 97-98--EIU.

text.p: Copper prices are forecast to decline this year and next as global stocks continue rising, the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) said in a report.
Consumption for copper is expected to grow in all the major economies, with growth forecasts revised upwards to 4.4 percent in 1997 and 4.6 percent in 1998.

"The higher forecasts reflect an increase in intensity of copper use in the 1990s...data for which indicate usage of copper to have grown faster than industrial production by 0.5 percent per year or more," the report said.
But supply of refined production is also expected to grow faster than first estimated, leading to a build in stocks.

Global stocks in 1996 rose by an estimated 25,000 tonnes, with Western stocks evidently falling by 150,000 tonnes and those elsewhere rising by 175,000 tonnes. Chinese reserves are thought to have increased by 175,000 to 200,000-300,000 tonnes.

"For 1997 and 1998 we predict an increase in global stocks of 375,000 tonnes. We have assumed that another 50,000 tonnes goes into the Chinese Strategic Reserve and that the rest builds up in the West," the report said.
Broken down by year, refined copper stocks were expected to come in at 1.7 million tonnes at the first quarter of 1997, 1.9 million tonnes in Q1 1998 and 2.075 million in Q1 1999.
Meanwhile prices were seen dipping by 1.5 percent year-on-year in 1997 to 102.5 cents/lb ($2,260 per tonne) on average, and falling 7.3 percent in 1998 to 95 cents/lb ($2,094).
In 1996 prices tumbled 21.9 percent to 104.1 cents/lb ($2,295).
The price forecasts assumed that China intends to prevent prices falling below 90 cent/lb ($1,984).
In the other metals markets, aluminium is expected to move into surplus from mid-1997 on higher production.
Nickel prices are forecast to fall as rising output overtakes grouth and demand, while lead's deficit in 1997 will shrink before the market moves into surplus in 1998/99.
Tin's longer-term prospects are seen bearish, with $6,300 per tonne as a ceiling, although currently prices are slightly too low.
Zinc's deficit is seen narrowing this year and next but the market will remain tight at least into the second half of 1998.
